abstract: "In League of Legends, players earn gold during a match and spend it on items that increase their character's damage. Using 2,795 ranked solo/duo games of the champion Jinx collected through the Riot Games application programming interface (API), I fit a simple linear regression of damage dealt to enemy champions per minute on gold earned per minute. Each additional 100 gold per minute is associated with about 315 more damage per minute, and gold income explains about 65% of the variation in damage output. Residual diagnostics show that the spread of damage grows with gold income, but the relationship is strong enough that this does not change the conclusion. The results give a simple baseline for how efficiently a typical Jinx player converts resources into damage, though they describe an association rather than a causal effect of gold."

```{r}
#| include: false
# load libraries: tidyverse for data wrangling + plots, knitr for tables
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)

# one row per jinx game, made by analysis/extract_jinx.R from the raw match files
raw <- read.csv("../output/jinx_gold_damage.csv")
```

```{r}
#| include: false
# cleaning. we flag each type of bad row first so the data section can
# report how many got dropped for each reason
n_raw <- nrow(raw)
n_other_queue <- sum(raw$queueId != 420)  # 420 = ranked solo/duo

# remakes: early-cancelled games or anything under 5 min (300 sec)
is_remake <- raw$earlySurrender | raw$gameDuration < 300
# off-role: jinx played somewhere other than bot lane
is_offrole <- !(raw$teamPosition %in% "BOTTOM")
# invalid: missing or negative gold/damage/length (just a safety check)
is_invalid <- !is.finite(raw$goldEarned) | !is.finite(raw$totalDamageDealtToChampions) |
  !is.finite(raw$gameDuration) | raw$goldEarned < 0 |
  raw$totalDamageDealtToChampions < 0

# count each drop reason without double counting rows that hit more than one
n_remake <- sum(is_remake)
n_offrole <- sum(!is_remake & is_offrole)
n_invalid <- sum(!is_remake & !is_offrole & is_invalid)

# keep the good rows and build the variables we actually use
jinx <- raw |>
  filter(queueId == 420, !is_remake, !is_offrole, !is_invalid) |>
  mutate(
    minutes = gameDuration / 60,                      # riot gives seconds
    gpm = goldEarned / minutes,                       # predictor: gold per min
    dpm = totalDamageDealtToChampions / minutes,      # response: damage per min
    patchMajor = as.integer(sub("\\..*", "", gameVersion)),  # "16.18.x" -> 16
    # gameCreation is a unix timestamp in milliseconds
    date = as.Date(as.POSIXct(gameCreation / 1000, origin = "1970-01-01",
                              tz = "UTC")),
    # order rank groups low -> elite so tables sort nicely
    rankBucket = factor(rankBucket, levels = c("low", "mid", "high", "elite"))
  )

# quick counts that get dropped into the text
n <- nrow(jinx)
players <- table(jinx$playerId)               # games per player
n_players <- length(players)
n_repeat_games <- sum(players[players > 1])   # games from people with 2+ games
pct_season16 <- mean(jinx$patchMajor == 16) * 100
region_counts <- table(jinx$platformId)

# per-minute rates don't fully remove game length, so compare the shortest
# and longest quarters of games for the data section
len_q <- quantile(jinx$minutes, c(0.25, 0.75))
short_games <- jinx |> filter(minutes <= len_q[1])
long_games <- jinx |> filter(minutes >= len_q[2])

# the main model: damage per minute regressed on gold per minute
lm_fit <- lm(dpm ~ gpm, data = jinx)
b <- coef(lm_fit)  # b[1] = intercept, b[2] = slope
```

# Introduction

In League of Legends [@league_of_legends], a team strategy game made by Riot Games, two teams of five players compete to destroy the other team's base. Before the match, each player picks a "champion", a character with its own abilities, from a pool of more than 160. Each player on a team usually fills one of five roles, and each role starts in a different area of the map: top lane, jungle, middle lane, and the bottom lane, which is shared by a marksman and a support. A typical match lasts 25 to 35 minutes. During a match, each player earns gold by killing computer-controlled minions and monsters, killing or helping to kill enemy champions, and destroying enemy structures, and a small amount of gold also arrives automatically over time. Players spend gold on items, which permanently increase their champion's attack damage, attack speed, health, and other attributes. A completed item costs roughly 3,000 gold, and a champion can hold six. Players and coaches often talk about gold as the currency of the game: a player who is "ahead" has more gold, more items, and therefore more ability to damage opponents.

Jinx is a marksman champion [@riot_jinx]. Marksmen deal most of their damage with repeated ranged basic attacks, which are weak early in the match and grow much stronger as the player buys items. Marksmen therefore depend more heavily on gold than most other roles, and Jinx is a common example of this style. This makes her a natural case for asking how strongly gold income and damage output are related.

Most published statistical work on League of Legends studies professional matches and models team-level outcomes such as winning. For example, @novak2020 modelled performance at the 2018 World Championship using team statistics. Professional games are a small and unusual sample, and team-level models do not describe how one player's resources relate to that player's output. Ranked solo/duo games cover millions of ordinary players, and the Riot Games application programming interface (API) [@riot_match_v5], a service that lets registered developers download game records, makes per-player statistics from those games available. I found no simple, published estimate of how much damage a typical ranked player on a single champion produces per unit of gold.

In this project I fit a simple linear regression of Jinx's damage to champions per minute on her gold earned per minute, using `r format(n, big.mark = ",")` ranked games from three server regions and all rank tiers. I restrict the analysis to one champion so that the slope is not driven by differences between champions (for example, support champions earn little gold and deal little damage by design). The estimated slope is about `r round(b[2], 2)` damage per gold: a Jinx player earning 100 more gold per minute deals about `r round(100 * b[2])` more damage per minute on average. The relationship is strong but not perfectly linear, and the variability of damage grows with gold. The estimate gives players and analysts a baseline for judging whether a given game's damage is high or low for the gold earned.

@sec-data introduces the data and the cleaning steps. @sec-methods describes the model, its assumptions, and how I checked them. @sec-results presents the fitted model and diagnostics, and @sec-discussion discusses what the results mean, their limitations, and possible extensions.

# Data {#sec-data}

## Source and collection

The data come from the Riot Games Match-V5 API [@riot_match_v5], which returns a detailed record of each completed match, including end-of-game statistics for all ten participants. Riot provides this data to registered developers under its API policies [@riot_api_policies]. In ranked play, each player's account is placed on a ladder of ten tiers, from Iron (lowest) through Bronze, Silver, Gold, Platinum, Emerald, Diamond, Master, and Grandmaster to Challenger (highest). Players move up by winning and down by losing, and matchmaking places players of similar rating in the same match. In the solo/duo queue, a player can enter alone or with one friend. I collected matches with a Python script in the project repository. The script samples ranked players from Riot's league ladders in three server regions (North America, Europe West, and Korea) and four rank groups: low (Iron to Silver), mid (Gold to Platinum), high (Emerald to Diamond), and elite (Master to Challenger). Within each group, players are drawn at random across all divisions. For each sampled player, the script downloads their 20 most recent ranked solo/duo matches. In total, `r format(21860, big.mark = ",")` matches were collected. Jinx appears in `r format(n_raw, big.mark = ",")` of them, and after the cleaning steps below, `r format(n, big.mark = ",")` games remain for the analysis. The sampled player is usually not the Jinx player: a sampled player's match history is only used to find matches, and any match that contains Jinx is kept, whoever played her.

Because matchmaking pairs players of similar skill, I label each match with the rank group of the sampled player it was downloaded for, which approximates the skill level of the whole match. Ranked players are not spread evenly across these groups: most accounts are in the lower and middle tiers, and Master and above holds only a small fraction of players. Because the script samples the same number of players from each rank group, games from higher ranks, especially the elite group, are over-represented in the sample relative to the player population. @sec-results checks whether this changes the estimated slope. Most games (`r round(pct_season16)`%) were played on patches from the 2026 season (version 16), so the data mostly reflect one version of the game.

## Observational units and cleaning

The observational unit is one Jinx player in one match. A champion can be picked by at most one player per ranked match, so each match contributes at most one row. `r if (n_other_queue == 0) "All" else paste("All but", n_other_queue, "of the")` `r format(n_raw, big.mark = ",")` matches containing Jinx are ranked solo/duo games (Riot queue 420). From these, I removed:

-   `r n_remake` games that ended in a "remake" (an early vote to cancel the match, usually because a player disconnected) or lasted under five minutes. Their statistics are near zero and do not reflect a played game.
-   `r n_offrole` games where Jinx was not played in the bottom lane. Jinx in another role faces different opponents and earns gold differently, and these games are too few to study separately.

`r if (n_invalid == 0) "No remaining rows had" else paste(n_invalid, "remaining rows had")` missing or negative values for the variables used`r if (n_invalid == 0) "" else ", and I removed them"`. The final dataset has `r format(n, big.mark = ",")` games from `r format(n_players, big.mark = ",")` distinct players; only `r n_repeat_games` games come from players who appear more than once.

## Variables

-   **Gold per minute** (`gpm`, the predictor) is `goldEarned`, the total gold the player earned during the match, divided by the match length in minutes. Gold earned includes gold from minions, monsters, kills, assists, objectives, and passive income over time.
-   **Damage per minute** (`dpm`, the response) is `totalDamageDealtToChampions`, the total damage the player dealt to enemy champions, divided by match length in minutes. It excludes damage to minions, monsters, and structures.
-   **Match length** (`gameDuration`) is recorded by Riot in seconds.

I use per-minute rates instead of totals because both gold and damage accumulate over time. With totals, a long game would have high values of both variables even for a poor performance, and the regression would mostly measure game length. Per-minute rates reduce this problem but do not remove it, because a marksman's damage grows as she completes items later in the game. In the shortest quarter of games (under `r round(len_q[1])` minutes), Jinx averages `r round(mean(short_games$dpm))` damage per minute, compared with `r round(mean(long_games$dpm))` in the longest quarter (over `r round(len_q[2])` minutes). Gold per minute changes much less, from `r round(mean(short_games$gpm))` to `r round(mean(long_games$gpm))`, so game length affects the response more than the predictor. Both variables are recorded automatically by the game server, so measurement error from data entry is not a concern. However, `totalDamageDealtToChampions` counts damage dealt, not damage that led to kills, so it is an imperfect measure of useful output.

#| fig-height: 3
# stack gpm and dpm into one long column so we can facet them side by side
jinx |>
  select(`Gold per minute` = gpm, `Damage to champions per minute` = dpm) |>
  pivot_longer(everything()) |>
  mutate(name = fct_inorder(name)) |>  # keep gold on the left, damage on the right
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +

@fig-hist shows the distribution of each variable. Gold per minute has a mean of `r round(mean(jinx$gpm))` and a standard deviation of `r round(sd(jinx$gpm))`. Damage per minute has a mean of `r round(mean(jinx$dpm))` and a standard deviation of `r round(sd(jinx$dpm))`, and it is right-skewed: a few games have very high damage, but damage cannot fall below zero.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-rank
#| tbl-cap: "Summary of the cleaned Jinx games by rank group of the match, with average gold per minute, damage per minute, game length and win rate. Rank groups are low (Iron to Silver), mid (Gold to Platinum), high (Emerald to Diamond), and elite (Master to Challenger). Average gold and damage per minute rise with rank, except that elite games have slightly lower damage than high games."
# one row per rank group with counts and averages
jinx |>
  group_by(Rank = rankBucket) |>
  summarise(
    Games = n(),
    `Gold/min` = round(mean(gpm)),
    `Damage/min` = round(mean(dpm)),
    `Length (min)` = round(mean(minutes), 1),
    `Win %` = round(100 * mean(win), 1)  # win is TRUE/FALSE so mean = win rate
  ) |>
  kable()
```

@tbl-rank breaks the sample down by rank group. The groups are close to evenly represented, and average gold per minute increases with rank, so rank is one source of variation in the predictor. Elite games are the shortest on average, which likely explains why their damage per minute is lower than in high games despite higher gold income.

Riot's API also provides minute-by-minute match timelines, and third-party sites such as League of Graphs [@leagueofgraphs] publish aggregate champion statistics. I use end-of-game statistics because they are complete for every match and match the question about a player's overall game.

# Methods {#sec-methods}

## Model

I fit the simple linear regression model [@kutner2005, Ch. 1]

$$Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad i = 1, \dots, n,$$

where $n =$ `r format(n, big.mark = ",")` is the number of games, $Y_i$ is Jinx's damage to champions per minute in game $i$, $X_i$ is her gold earned per minute in game $i$, treated as a known constant, and $\varepsilon_i$ is a random error with mean zero and finite variance $\sigma^2$, with errors independent across games. The error represents everything else that affects damage in that game, such as the player's skill, item choices, and the opposing team. Under this model, the mean damage per minute in games with gold per minute $X_i$ is $E(Y_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i$, and the variance around that mean is $\mathrm{Var}(Y_i) = \sigma^2$.

The slope $\beta_1$ is the change in mean damage per minute for each one-unit increase in gold per minute. The intercept $\beta_0$ is the mean damage per minute when gold per minute is zero. No real game has zero gold income (the minimum in the data is `r round(min(jinx$gpm))`), so $\beta_0$ positions the line and has no practical meaning on its own.

I chose gold as the predictor and damage as the response because gold buys items, and items increase damage. The reverse also happens, because damage leads to kills, which pay gold. The model therefore describes an association and cannot estimate the causal effect of giving a player more gold.

## Estimation and inference

I estimate $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ by ordinary least squares (OLS), where the estimates $b_0$ and $b_1$ are the values of $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ that minimize $Q = \sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 X_i)^2$. The fitted value for game $i$ is $\widehat{Y}_i = b_0 + b_1 X_i$, and the residual is $e_i = Y_i - \widehat{Y}_i$. I estimate $\sigma^2$ with $s^2 = \mathrm{MSE} = \mathrm{SSE}/(n - 2)$, where $\mathrm{SSE} = \sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2$, and call $s$ the residual standard error. The coefficient of determination $R^2 = 1 - \mathrm{SSE}/\mathrm{SSTO}$, where $\mathrm{SSTO} = \sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \overline{Y})^2$, is the proportion of the variation in damage per minute explained by the fitted line.

I test $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$ against $H_A: \beta_1 \neq 0$ with a type I error rate of $\alpha = 0.05$, using the test statistic $t^* = b_1 / \widehat{\mathrm{se}}(b_1)$, where $\widehat{\mathrm{se}}(b_1) = s / \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \overline{X})^2}$. Under the normal error regression model and $H_0$, $t^*$ follows a $t(n-2)$ distribution, and I reject $H_0$ if $|t^*| > t_{0.975,\, n-2}$. A 95% confidence interval for $\beta_1$ is $b_1 \pm t_{0.975,\, n-2} \times \widehat{\mathrm{se}}(b_1)$.

Following @gelman2020 [Ch. 11], I consider the assumptions of the analysis in decreasing order of importance:

1.  **Validity:** the variables measure what the question is about. Damage to champions counts all damage dealt, not only damage that decided a fight. This is needed for the slope to answer the research question at all.
2.  **Representativeness:** the sample resembles all ranked Jinx games. This is needed to generalize the estimate beyond the sampled games. Higher ranks are over-sampled (@sec-data), which matters only if the relationship differs by rank.
3.  **Linearity:** $E(Y_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i$. This is needed for $b_1$ to describe how mean damage changes with gold; if the true trend is curved, a single slope summarizes it poorly.
4.  **Independence:** the errors $\varepsilon_i$ are independent across games. This is needed for the standard error of $b_1$, and therefore the test and confidence interval, to be correct.
5.  **Equal variance:** the errors have the same variance $\sigma^2$ at every value of $X_i$. This is also needed for the usual standard error to be correct; without it, $b_1$ is still unbiased.
6.  **Normality:** the errors are normally distributed. This is needed for $t^*$ to follow an exact $t(n-2)$ distribution. With thousands of games, the central limit theorem makes the test approximately valid even without it.

Following @kutner2005 [Ch. 3], I check linearity and equal variance with a plot of residuals against fitted values, and normality with a normal quantile-quantile (Q-Q) plot. I check representativeness by refitting the model within each rank group. Independence is mostly supported by the design, since each match contributes one Jinx player. However, `r n_repeat_games` games come from players who appear more than once, and two games by the same player are likely to share that player's skill and habits, which technically violates independence. To check whether this matters, I refit the model using only each player's earliest game.

A single predictor leaves out other influences on damage, such as rank. Adding rank as a second predictor could move the slope in either direction, and modelling $\log Y_i$ could make the variance more equal. I return to these extensions in @sec-discussion.

## Software

I performed the analysis in R [@R_language]. The raw JSON match files were read with the `jsonlite` package, and the data were processed and plotted with the `tidyverse` [@tidyverse]. I fit the regression model with R's `lm()` function. The project report was written in Quarto.

# Results {#sec-results}

```{r}
#| include: false
# pull out the stuff the results section talks about
ci <- confint(lm_fit)       # 95% confidence intervals for b0 and b1
fit_sum <- summary(lm_fit)  # has the t stat, r^2, residual standard error, etc

e <- resid(lm_fit)  # residuals = observed - fitted

# refit the same model inside each rank group to see if the slope changes a lot
# (checks whether over-sampling higher ranks messes with the overall slope)
rank_fits <- jinx |>
  group_by(rankBucket) |>
  group_modify(~ tibble(slope = coef(lm(dpm ~ gpm, data = .x))[2])) |>
  ungroup()

# refit with one game per player (their earliest) to check that players who
# show up more than once aren't driving the slope (independence check)
one_per_player <- jinx |>
  arrange(gameCreation) |>
  distinct(playerId, .keep_all = TRUE)
slope_one <- coef(lm(dpm ~ gpm, data = one_per_player))[2]

# split fitted values into low/middle/high thirds and get the residual sd in
# each one. if the sd grows across thirds, the equal variance assumption is off
fit_terciles <- cut(fitted(lm_fit), quantile(fitted(lm_fit), 0:3 / 3),
                    include.lowest = TRUE)
resid_sd <- tapply(e, fit_terciles, sd)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-scatter
#| fig-cap: "Damage to champions per minute against gold earned per minute for 2,795 ranked Jinx games, with the fitted least-squares line (red). Games with more gold income have higher damage output, and the points spread out more at higher gold income."
#| fig-height: 4
# scatter of every game with the least-squares line on top
ggplot(jinx, aes(x = gpm, y = dpm)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2, size = 0.8) +  # see-through dots so overlap shows up darker
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "red") +  # same line as lm_fit
  labs(x = "Gold earned per minute", y = "Damage to champions per minute") +
  theme_classic()
```

@fig-scatter shows a strong positive linear relationship between gold and damage per minute; the sample correlation is `r sprintf("%.2f", cor(jinx$gpm, jinx$dpm))`. The fitted regression line is

`r sprintf("$$\\widehat{Y} = %.1f + %.3f X.$$", b[1], b[2])`

```{r}
#| label: tbl-coef
#| tbl-cap: "Estimated coefficients for the regression of damage to champions per minute on gold earned per minute (n = 2,795). The 95% confidence interval for the slope is far from zero."
# build the coefficient table by hand instead of printing raw summary() output
tibble(
  Term = c("Intercept ($b_0$)", "Gold per minute ($b_1$)"),
  Estimate = c(sprintf("%.1f", b[1]), sprintf("%.3f", b[2])),  # 1 decimal for the intercept, 3 for the slope
  `Std. error` = fit_sum$coefficients[, "Std. Error"],
  `95% CI` = sprintf("(%.2f, %.2f)", ci[, 1], ci[, 2])
) |>
  kable(digits = 3, escape = FALSE, align = "lrrl")  # escape = FALSE so the $b_0$ math renders
```

The estimated slope is $b_1 =$ `r round(b[2], 3)` (@tbl-coef). For each additional gold earned per minute, the expected damage to champions per minute increases by about `r round(b[2], 2)`. On a more useful scale, a Jinx player who earns 100 more gold per minute, roughly one standard deviation, deals about `r round(100 * b[2])` more damage per minute on average. The estimated intercept is $b_0 =$ `r round(b[1], 1)`. A negative damage value is impossible, which confirms that the intercept only positions the line and should not be interpreted directly.

The $t$-statistic for $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$ is $t^* =$ `r round(fit_sum$coefficients[2, "t value"], 1)` with `r format(fit_sum$df[2], big.mark = ",")` degrees of freedom, giving a $p$-value below $10^{-15}$, so I reject $H_0$ at $\alpha = 0.05$: gold and damage per minute are linearly associated. The 95% confidence interval for $\beta_1$ is (`r round(ci[2, 1], 2)`, `r round(ci[2, 2], 2)`), a narrow range of plausible values for the slope. The coefficient of determination is $R^2 =$ `r round(fit_sum$r.squared, 3)`, so gold per minute accounts for about `r round(100 * fit_sum$r.squared)`% of the variation in damage per minute. The residual standard error is $s =$ `r round(fit_sum$sigma)` damage per minute, so a typical game is about `r round(fit_sum$sigma)` damage per minute above or below the line.

```{r}
#| label: fig-resid
#| fig-cap: "Residuals against fitted values for the regression of damage per minute on gold per minute. The dashed line marks zero and the blue curve is a smoothed trend. The vertical spread of the residuals increases from left to right, showing that the error variance grows with predicted damage. The curve bends slightly upward at both ends, showing mild curvature."
#| fig-height: 3.5
# residuals vs fitted: checks linearity (trend should hug 0) and equal variance
# (spread should stay about the same left to right)
tibble(fitted = fitted(lm_fit), resid = e) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = fitted, y = resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2, size = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, colour = "steelblue") +  # smooth trend line
  labs(x = "Fitted damage per minute", y = "Residual (observed - fitted)") +
  theme_classic()
```

@fig-resid checks the linearity and equal-variance assumptions. The residuals are centred near zero across most of the fitted range, with a mild upward bend at both ends, so a straight line describes the trend well. Their spread increases, however: the residual standard deviation is `r round(resid_sd[1])` in the lowest third of fitted values, `r round(resid_sd[2])` in the middle third, and `r round(resid_sd[3])` in the highest third, so the equal-variance assumption is not met.

```{r}
#| label: fig-qq
#| fig-cap: "Normal Q-Q plot of the regression residuals. Points on the line would indicate normally distributed errors. The upper tail rises above the line, showing that the residuals are right-skewed: some games have much more damage than predicted, while very large shortfalls are less common."
#| fig-height: 3.5
# normal q-q plot: if residuals were normal the dots would sit on the red line
tibble(resid = e) |>
  ggplot(aes(sample = resid)) +
  stat_qq(alpha = 0.3, size = 0.8) +
  stat_qq_line(colour = "red") +
  labs(x = "Theoretical normal quantiles", y = "Residual quantiles") +
  theme_classic()
```

@fig-qq shows that the residuals are right-skewed, so the normality assumption is also not met. With `r format(n, big.mark = ",")` observations, the sampling distribution of $b_1$ is still close to normal by the central limit theorem, so this departure has little effect on the test. The unequal variance matters more, because the reported standard error assumes a constant $\sigma^2$ and is therefore only approximate. It would have to be more than `r floor(fit_sum$coefficients[2, "t value"] / qt(0.975, fit_sum$df[2]))` times too small for the slope to stop being significant, so the conclusion that gold and damage are positively associated does not depend on this assumption.

To check representativeness, I fit the same model separately within each rank group. The slopes range from `r sprintf("%.2f", min(rank_fits$slope))` (`r rank_fits$rankBucket[which.min(rank_fits$slope)]`) to `r sprintf("%.2f", max(rank_fits$slope))` (`r rank_fits$rankBucket[which.max(rank_fits$slope)]`), all close to the pooled estimate, so over-representing higher ranks has little effect on the overall slope. To check independence, I refit the model using only each player's earliest game (`r format(nrow(one_per_player), big.mark = ",")` games). The slope is `r sprintf("%.2f", slope_one)`, nearly the same as the full-sample estimate of `r sprintf("%.2f", b[2])`, so the players who appear more than once do not change the conclusions.

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

This analysis asked how strongly a Jinx player's gold income is related to the damage she deals to enemy champions. In ranked solo/duo games across all skill levels, the relationship is strong and positive: 100 extra gold per minute goes with about `r round(100 * b[2])` extra damage per minute, and gold income explains about `r round(100 * fit_sum$r.squared)`% of the variation in damage. For players and coaches, the fitted line gives a simple benchmark for average output at a given gold income. A game far below the line suggests the player earned gold but did not turn it into damage, for example because of poor positioning or spending too much time away from fights. The remaining `r round(100 * (1 - fit_sum$r.squared))`% of unexplained variation, and the growing spread at high gold, show that gold alone does not determine output: two players with the same gold can deal very different amounts of damage.

The main strengths of the analysis are its large sample across three regions and four rank groups, the use of per-minute rates to reduce the effect of game length, and the focus on one champion, which avoids comparing champions built for different roles.

There are also weaknesses. First, the relationship runs in both directions: gold buys items that raise damage, but damage also produces kills that pay gold. The slope therefore mixes both effects and should not be read as the damage that extra gold would cause. Second, the sample of players is not a simple random sample of all Jinx games. Players were drawn from rank ladders in equal numbers per rank group, so low-ranked games, which make up most real games, are under-represented relative to the player population. The slopes are similar across rank groups, which limits the effect of this imbalance. Third, the error variance is not constant, and the relationship has mild curvature, so predictions for games with very high gold are less precise than the residual standard error suggests. Fourth, the rank label comes from the sampled player, not the Jinx player. Fifth, per-minute rates do not fully remove game length: damage per minute is higher in longer games, so part of the variation the model attributes to gold may come from game length instead.

Several extensions could address these issues. The match timelines already downloaded for this project record gold and damage minute by minute, so gold at 15 minutes could be used to predict later damage, reducing the feedback from damage to gold. Adding rank group as a predictor in a multiple regression would show whether the slope differs across skill levels, and adding game length would separate the effect of gold from the late-game growth in damage. Repeating the analysis for other marksmen would show whether Jinx converts gold into damage more efficiently than similar champions.
